animals.blurb: Famous for their incredible 3,000-mile migration to Mexican forests. Their orange and black wings warn predators of the toxins they accumulate from milkweed. Now endangered.
animals.hint: An orange migrator that flies thousands of miles

animals.blurb: The most widespread butterfly in the world, found on every continent except Antarctica and Australia. They undergo massive irruptive migrations in some years.
animals.hint: The most widespread butterfly on Earth

animals.blurb: Large, striking butterflies with yellow wings marked by black tiger stripes. Females can also occur in a dark form. They are strong fliers often seen 'puddling' on wet ground.
animals.hint: A large yellow butterfly with black tiger stripes

animals.blurb: Their caterpillars feed on parsley, dill, and carrots in gardens. When threatened, caterpillars extend a forked, foul-smelling orange organ called an osmeterium.
animals.hint: A garden swallowtail whose caterpillars love parsley

animals.blurb: An introduced species from Europe, now one of the most common butterflies. Their caterpillars are garden pests on cabbages and related crops.
animals.hint: A common white butterfly that loves your vegetables

animals.blurb: Striking black butterflies with orange-red bands and white spots. They are territorial and often land on people. They feed on rotting fruit and tree sap.
animals.hint: A bold black butterfly with orange racing stripes

animals.blurb: Named for the prominent eyespots on their wings that startle predators. They cannot survive northern winters and recolonize each year from the south.
animals.hint: A butterfly with big eye spots that watch you back

animals.blurb: One of the most beautiful moths in North America, with large pale green wings and long trailing tails. Adults live only about a week and don't eat—they have no mouths.
animals.hint: A ghostly green giant that lives just one week

animals.blurb: North America's largest native moth, with wingspans reaching 6 inches. Like all giant silk moths, adults cannot eat and live only to reproduce.
animals.hint: The continent's largest moth with a 6-inch wingspan

animals.blurb: Named after the cyclops Polyphemus for the large eyespots on their hindwings. One of the most widespread giant silk moths, their caterpillars can eat 86,000 times their body weight.
animals.hint: A giant moth with cyclops-like eye spots

animals.blurb: The world's most important pollinator, responsible for pollinating roughly one-third of food crops. They communicate food locations through their famous 'waggle dance.'
animals.hint: The essential pollinator that dances to share secrets

animals.blurb: Fuzzy and buzzy, bumblebees are important pollinators that can fly in cooler temperatures than honey bees. They vibrate their flight muscles to warm up and 'buzz pollinate' flowers.
animals.hint: A fuzzy buzzer that works in cool weather

animals.blurb: These large bees bore holes in wood to nest, sometimes damaging structures. Males are harmless—they can't sting—but aggressively hover near anyone approaching nests.
animals.hint: A wood-boring bee that hovers but can't sting

animals.blurb: Aggressive wasps that nest underground or in wall voids. They're beneficial predators of pest insects but become problematic at picnics when seeking sugary foods in late summer.
animals.hint: A picnic crasher with a painful sting

animals.blurb: They build distinctive umbrella-shaped paper nests from chewed wood fibers. Less aggressive than yellow jackets, they help control caterpillar populations.
animals.hint: A wasp that builds paper umbrellas under your eaves

animals.blurb: Not true hornets but large yellow jackets with white faces. They build impressive football-sized paper nests in trees and fiercely defend them.
animals.hint: A white-faced wasp building giant paper footballs

animals.blurb: Europe's most common ladybug, introduced to North America for aphid control. A single ladybug can eat 5,000 aphids in its lifetime, making them garden heroes.
animals.hint: A red beetle with seven spots that devours aphids

animals.blurb: Introduced for pest control, these ladybugs now invade homes in fall by the thousands. They can bite and secrete a foul-smelling fluid when disturbed.
animals.hint: The ladybug that invades homes every autumn

animals.blurb: An invasive pest that skeletonizes leaves and damages lawns as larvae (white grubs). Their metallic green and copper coloring makes them beautiful but destructive.
animals.hint: A beautiful metallic pest that destroys gardens

animals.blurb: These clumsy, buzzing beetles emerge in early summer and are attracted to lights. Their larvae are the white grubs that damage lawns by feeding on grass roots.
animals.hint: A clumsy summer beetle that crashes into porch lights

animals.blurb: Magical summer beetles that produce light through bioluminescence to attract mates. Each species has a unique flash pattern. Populations are declining due to light pollution and habitat loss.
animals.hint: A living lantern flashing love signals at dusk

animals.blurb: Males have impressive antler-like mandibles used for wrestling rivals over females. Their larvae spend years in rotting wood before emerging as impressive adults.
animals.hint: A beetle with antlers that wrestles for mates

animals.blurb: Introduced from Asia, these large mantises are ambush predators that catch prey with lightning-fast strikes. Females sometimes eat males during mating.
animals.hint: A patient hunter with grasping prayer hands

animals.blurb: The only mantis species native to North America. Smaller than introduced species, they come in green, brown, and gray color forms.
animals.hint: America's only native praying mantis

animals.blurb: One of the largest and most common dragonflies in North America. They migrate in swarms and can fly at speeds over 30 mph while hunting mosquitoes and other flying insects.
animals.hint: A large migrating dragonfly that hunts at 30 mph

animals.blurb: Named for the twelve dark wing spots (three on each wing), males develop white patches between the spots. They perch conspicuously and patrol territories around ponds.
animals.hint: A dragonfly with polka-dotted wings

animals.blurb: A stunning damselfly with solid black wings. Males have iridescent green bodies while females have brown wings with white spots. They flutter gracefully along woodland streams.
animals.hint: A metallic damselfly with pure black wings

animals.blurb: Their buzzing calls are the soundtrack of hot summer days. Unlike periodical cicadas, they emerge every year. Nymphs spend 2-5 years underground feeding on tree roots.
animals.hint: The buzzing voice of hot summer afternoons

animals.blurb: Famous for emerging in massive numbers every 17 years (or 13 in southern broods). Billions emerge simultaneously, overwhelming predators and creating a deafening chorus.
animals.hint: A cicada that waits 17 years for one big party

animals.blurb: The classic black cricket whose chirping serenades late summer nights. You can estimate temperature by counting chirps—add 40 to the number of chirps in 14 seconds for Fahrenheit.
animals.hint: A black chirper that tells you the temperature

animals.blurb: Their loud 'katy-did, katy-didn't' calls fill summer nights from the treetops. Their leaf-shaped bodies make them nearly impossible to spot despite how loud they are.
animals.hint: A leaf-shaped singer arguing 'Katy did, Katy didn't'

animals.blurb: One of the largest grasshoppers in North America, reaching 2.5 inches. Related to plague locusts, they occasionally form damaging swarms but usually live solitary lives.
animals.hint: A large jumping insect related to plague locusts

animals.blurb: Masters of camouflage that look exactly like twigs. When disturbed, they simply drop to the ground and become invisible among leaf litter. All North American species lack wings.
animals.hint: A twig that walks away when you look too close

animals.blurb: Also called 'toe-biters,' these fierce predators can grow to 4 inches and deliver one of the most painful insect bites. They catch fish, frogs, and even small snakes.
animals.hint: A toe-biting terror that catches fish and frogs

animals.blurb: Named for the distinctive cog-wheel crest on their backs, wheel bugs are assassin bugs that ambush and stab prey with their sharp beaks. Their bite to humans is extremely painful.
animals.hint: A cog-wheeled predator with a painful stab

animals.blurb: Males are bright yellow while females are reddish-brown, but both flash dramatic eye spots when startled. Their spiny caterpillars deliver a painful, stinging sting.
animals.hint: A giant moth with startling owl-eye spots

animals.blurb: The fuzzy caterpillar famous for supposedly predicting winter severity (wider brown bands = milder winter). They overwinter as caterpillars and become plain Isabella Tiger Moths.
animals.hint: A fuzzy caterpillar that folklore says predicts winter

animals.blurb: Huge green caterpillars that devastate tomato plants overnight. They transform into five-spotted hawk moths. Caterpillars covered in white cocoons are being parasitized by beneficial wasps.
animals.hint: A giant green caterpillar eating your tomatoes
